Convergence of the one-dimensional Cahn-Hilliard equation

Giovanni Bellettini Address: Dipartimento di Matematica, Università di Roma Tor Vergata, via della Ricerca Scientifica 1, 00133 Roma, Italy. Email address: belletti@mat.uniroma2.it , Lorenzo Bertini Address: Dipartimento di Matematica, Università di Roma La Sapienza, Piazzale Aldo Moro 2, 00185 Roma, Italy. Email address: bertini@mat.uniroma1.it , Mauro Mariani Address: Laboratoire d’Analyse, Topologie, Probabilités (CNRS UMR 6632), Université Aix-Marseille, Avenue Escadrille Normandie-Niemen, 13397 Marseille Cedex 20, France. Email address: mariani@cmi.univ-mrs.fr and Matteo Novaga Address: Dipartimento di Matematica, Università di Padova, via Trieste 63, 35121 Padova, Italy. Email address: novaga@math.unipd.it
Abstract.

We consider the Cahn-Hilliard equation in one space dimension with scaling parameter ε\varepsilon, i.e. ut=(W′​(u)−ε2​ux​x)x​xu_{t}=(W^{\prime}(u)-\varepsilon^{2}u_{xx})_{xx}, where WW is a nonconvex potential. In the limit ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0, under the assumption that the initial data are energetically well-prepared, we show the convergence to a Stefan problem. The proof is based on variational methods and exploits the gradient flow structure of the Cahn-Hilliard equation.

1. Introduction

In this paper we are interested in the convergence of solutions uε=uε​(⋅,⋅,u¯ε){u_{\varepsilon}}={u_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,\cdot,\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}) to the equation

{ut=(W′​(u)−ε2​ux​x)x​xin (0,+∞)×𝕋u=u¯εon {0}×𝕋\begin{cases}{\rm u}_{t}=\big(W^{\prime}({\rm u})-\varepsilon^{2}{\rm u}_{xx}\big)_{xx}&\text{in $(0,+\infty)\times{\mathbb{T}}$}\\ {\rm u}=\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}&\text{on $\{0\}\times\mathbb{T}$}\end{cases} (1.1)

as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0, where 𝕋:=ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{T}:={\mathbb{R}}/{\mathbb{Z}} is the one-dimensional torus. Here ε\varepsilon is a spatial scale parameter and WW is a rather general smooth potential. Our analysis covers, in particular, the choice of the double-well potential

W⁡(ξ)=(1−ξ2)24ξ∈ℝ,W(\xi)=\frac{(1-\xi^{2})^{2}}{4}\qquad\xi\in\mathbb{R}, (1.2)

corresponding to the Cahn-Hilliard equation. We refer for instance to [5, 8] for the physical motivations leading to equation (1.1), in relation with the theory of phase transitions, and to [18, 2, 6] for some mathematical results and connections with the Stefan problem [14].

Equation (1.1) can be seen as the gradient flow, in the H−1H^{-1}-topology, of the Allen-Cahn type functional

Fε​(v)=∫𝕋(ε2​vx22+W⁡(v))​𝑑x,{F_{\varepsilon}}(v)=\int_{\mathbb{T}}\left(\varepsilon^{2}\frac{v_{x}^{2}}{2}+W(v)\right)dx, (1.3)

where the scalar field vv represents the local order parameter. The gradient flow structure of (1.1) allows us to look at the convergence of the functions uε{u_{\varepsilon}} in a purely variational way, at least under the assumption of energetically well-prepared initial data.

The main difficulty in studying the limit of uε{u_{\varepsilon}} is due to the fact that, when the function WW is nonconvex, (1.1) is forward-backward parabolic for ε=0\varepsilon=0. Looking at equation (1.1), it is rather natural to expect a limit equation related to the H−1H^{-1}-gradient flow of the functional

F⁡(v)=∫𝕋W⁡(v)​𝑑x.F(v)=\int_{\mathbb{T}}W(v)~dx. (1.4)

However, when WW is nonconvex, the functional FF is not convex and not lower semicontinuous with respect to the H−1H^{-1}-topology, and the gradient flow dynamics is not well-posed. The lower semicontinuous envelope of FF is given by

F∗⁣∗​(v)=∫𝕋W∗⁣∗​(v)​𝑑x,{F^{**}}(v)=\int_{\mathbb{T}}W^{**}(v)~dx,

where W∗⁣∗W^{**} denotes the convex envelope of WW. It is not difficult to prove (see Proposition A.1) that F∗⁣∗{F^{**}} is the Γ\Gamma-limit of the functionals Fε{F_{\varepsilon}} as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0, with respect to the H−1H^{-1}-topology.

In this paper we prove that the solutions uε{u_{\varepsilon}} to (1.1) converge to the gradient flow of F∗⁣∗{F^{**}}, as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0, under a suitable assumption on the initial data u¯ε\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}. Our main result can be informally stated as follows (see Theorem 3.2 for the precise statement). Let u¯\overline{u} be such that F∗⁣∗​(u¯)<+∞{F^{**}}(\overline{u})<+\infty, take a sequence (u¯ε)(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}) of initial data satisfying Fε​(u¯ε)<+∞{F_{\varepsilon}}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon})<+\infty, converging to u¯\overline{u} in H−1​(𝕋)H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}) such that

∫𝕋u¯ε​𝑑x=∫𝕋u¯​𝑑x,\int_{\mathbb{T}}\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}~dx=\int_{\mathbb{T}}\overline{u}~dx,

and

limε↓0Fε​(u¯ε)=F∗⁣∗​(u¯).\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}{F_{\varepsilon}}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon})={F^{**}}(\overline{u}). (1.5)

Then the solution uε​(⋅,⋅,u¯ε){u_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,\cdot,\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}) of (1.1) converges to the H−1H^{-1}-gradient flow of F∗⁣∗{F^{**}}, namely to the solution uu of

{∂tu=(W∗∗′(u))x​xin (0,+∞)×𝕋u=u¯on {0}×𝕋,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\big(W^{**~\!\prime}(u)\big)_{xx}&\text{in $(0,+\infty)\times{\mathbb{T}}$}\\ u=\overline{u}&\text{on $\{0\}\times{\mathbb{T}}$},\end{cases} (1.6)

which, for WW nonconvex, is the weak formulation of the Stefan problem [14].

Some comments concerning hypothesis (1.5) are in order, related to the so-called wrinkling phenomenon. Given u¯∈H−1​(𝕋)\overline{u}\in H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}), define

ΣG:={ξ∈ℝ:W⁡(ξ)>W∗⁣∗​(ξ)},ΣL:={ξ∈ℝ:W′′​(ξ)<0},\Sigma_{G}:=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}:W(\xi)>W^{**}(\xi)\},\qquad\Sigma_{L}:=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}:W^{\prime\prime}(\xi)<0\}, (1.7)

and

ΣG​(u¯):={x∈𝕋:u¯​(x)∈ΣG},ΣL​(u¯):={x∈𝕋:u¯​(x)∈ΣL}.\Sigma_{G}(\overline{u}):=\{x\in\mathbb{T}:\overline{u}(x)\in\Sigma_{G}\},\qquad\Sigma_{L}(\overline{u}):=\{x\in\mathbb{T}:\overline{u}(x)\in\Sigma_{L}\}.

We call ΣG​(u¯)\Sigma_{G}(\overline{u}) the global unstable set of u¯\overline{u}, and ΣL​(u¯)\Sigma_{L}(\overline{u}) the local unstable set of u¯\overline{u}. Numerical simulations performed in [3] (see also [11]) show a quick formation of oscillations and these microstructures seem to generically appear only in ΣL​(u¯)\Sigma_{L}(\overline{u}), instead that on the whole of ΣG​(u¯)\Sigma_{G}(\overline{u}). In addition, superimposing on u¯\overline{u} a microstructure in a region Σ⊆ΣG​(u¯)∖ΣL​(u¯)\Sigma\subseteq\Sigma_{G}(\overline{u})\setminus\Sigma_{L}(\overline{u}) leads to a numerical solution which seems to depend on the choice of Σ\Sigma. These simulations show an instability of solutions uε​(⋅,⋅,u¯){u_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,\cdot,\overline{u}) with respect to u¯\overline{u}. In particular, if we take two sequences (u~ε)(\widetilde{u}_{\varepsilon}), (u^ε)(\widehat{u}_{\varepsilon}) of initial data both approximating u¯\overline{u} and corresponding to two different choices of Σ\Sigma, in general one may expect that

limε↓0uε​(⋅,⋅,(u~ε))≠limε↓0uε​(⋅,⋅,(u^ε)).\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}{u_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,\cdot,(\widetilde{u}_{\varepsilon}))~\neq~\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}{u_{\varepsilon}}(\cdot,\cdot,(\widehat{u}_{\varepsilon})).

Hypothesis (1.5) can thus be interpreted as an energetically well-prepared assumption on the initial data u¯ε\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}, corresponding to the choice of the above mentioned region Σ=ΣG​(u¯)∖ΣL​(u¯)\Sigma=\Sigma_{G}(\overline{u})\setminus\Sigma_{L}(\overline{u}). It is worth to remark that, in view of the Γ\Gamma-limit Fε→F∗⁣∗F_{\varepsilon}\to F^{**} stated above, given any u¯∈H−1\overline{u}\in H^{-1}, there exists a sequence (u¯ε)(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}) converging to u¯\overline{u} and satisfying (1.5).

The proof of our main result is entirely variational, and it is worthwhile to observe that we never use directly equation (1.1). The main point, indeed, is to derive sufficient information on a sequence (vε)(v_{\varepsilon}) of functions (independent of time) satisfying the uniform bound

supε∈(0,1]{Fε​(vε)+∫𝕋[(W′​(vε)−ε2​vεx​x)x]2​𝑑x}<+∞.\sup_{\varepsilon\in(0,1]}\left\{{F_{\varepsilon}}(v_{\varepsilon})+\int_{\mathbb{T}}\Big[~\Big(W^{\prime}(v_{\varepsilon})-\varepsilon^{2}{v_{\varepsilon}}_{xx}\Big)_{x}~\Big]^{2}~dx\right\}<+\infty. (1.8)

We follow an idea formalized by E. Sandier and S. Serfaty in [17] (see also [16]), where it is shown that the convergence of the gradient flows of a sequence of functionals ℱε:H→[0,+∞]\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}:H\to[0,+\infty], where HH is a Hilbert space, to the gradient flow of ℱ:=Γ−limℱε\mathcal{F}:=\Gamma-\lim\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon} is basically a consequence of the Γ\Gamma-convergence of the sequence of the slopes of the gradients |∇ℱε||\nabla\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}| of ℱε\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon} to the slope of the gradient |∇ℱ||\nabla\mathcal{F}| of ℱ\mathcal{F}. More precisely, it suffices to show the Γ\Gamma-liminf inequality

Γ−lim infε→0|∇ℱε|≥|∇ℱ|.\Gamma-\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}\ |\nabla\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}|\ \geq\ |\nabla\mathcal{F}|. (1.9)

The above inequality, in our setting, is the content of Theorem 3.3. We then obtain the corresponding convergence of the gradient flows of Fε{F_{\varepsilon}} in Theorem 3.2. The main difficulty in the proof is contained in Lemma 5.1, where a careful analysis of the regions where the functions vεv_{\varepsilon} oscillate is performed.

We mention that the same method proposed in [17] has been successfully applied in [12, 13] to show the convergence, in all space dimensions, of solutions to the rescaled Cahn-Hilliard equation

{ut=Δ⁡(ε−1​W′​(u)−ε​Δ​u)u⁡(0,⋅)=u¯ε,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta\big(\varepsilon^{-1}W^{\prime}(u)-\varepsilon\Delta u\big)\\ u(0,\cdot)=\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\end{cases}

under suitable simplifying assumptions, in particular related to the validity of the analog of (1.9).

We observe that equation (1.1) is not the only way to regularize the ill-posed gradient flow equation of the functional (1.4): other regularizations have been considered in the literature, see for instance [15, 7, 10, 9, 19]. In particular, in [7] it is proposed an implicit variational scheme for the functional (1.4) which converges to (1.6) as the discretization parameter tends to zero. Due to the high instability of the problem, different regularizations could in principle lead to different limiting solutions.

2. Notation

Let 𝕋:=ℝ/ℤ{\mathbb{T}}:={\mathbb{R}}/{\mathbb{Z}} be the one-dimensional torus of side length 11, and d​xdx be the Lebesgue measure on 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}. For m∈ℝm\in{\mathbb{R}}, let

ℋm−1​(𝕋):={v∈H−1​(𝕋):⟨v,1⟩=m}{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}):=\big\{v\in H^{-1}(\mathbb{T})\,:\>\langle v,1\rangle=m\}

where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the H−1​(𝕋)H^{-1}({\mathbb{T}})-H1​(𝕋)H^{1}({\mathbb{T}}) duality. ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) is a closed affine subspace of H−1​(𝕋)H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}), that will be considered equipped with the induced metric. The linear space associated with ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) is the homogeneous negative Sobolev space

H˙−1​(𝕋)∼ℋ0−1​(𝕋).\dot{H}^{-1}({\mathbb{T}})\sim\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{0}(\mathbb{T}).

In the following, we denote by ∥⋅∥−1\|\cdot\|_{-1} the Hilbert norm on H˙−1​(𝕋)\dot{H}^{-1}({\mathbb{T}}), namely

‖v‖−12:=‖v‖H˙−1​(𝕋)2=supφ∈H1​(𝕋){2​⟨v,φ⟩−‖φx‖L2​(𝕋)2},\|v\|_{-1}^{2}:=\|v\|_{\dot{H}^{-1}({\mathbb{T}})}^{2}=\sup_{\varphi\in H^{1}({\mathbb{T}})}\left\{2\langle v,\varphi\rangle-\|\varphi_{x}\|_{L^{2}({\mathbb{T}})}^{2}\right\}, (2.1)

and we understand ‖v‖−1:=+∞\|v\|_{-1}:=+\infty if v∉H˙−1​(𝕋)v\not\in\dot{H}^{-1}({\mathbb{T}}).

Throughout the paper, we use the term sequence also to denote families labeled by the continuous positive parameter ε\varepsilon. A subsequence of (fε)(f_{\varepsilon}) is a sequence (fεh)(f_{\varepsilon_{h}}) with εh↓0\varepsilon_{h}\downarrow 0 as h→+∞h\to+\infty.

2.1. Assumptions on WW

In the sequel we assume that WW is a function in 𝒞2(ℝ;[0,+∞))\mathcal{C}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};[0,+\infty)) satisfying the following properties:

  1. i)

    there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

    |W′​(ξ)|≤C⁡(1+W⁡(ξ)),ξ∈ℝ,|W^{\prime}(\xi)|\leq C(1+W(\xi)),\qquad\xi\in\mathbb{R}, (2.2)

    and

    lim|ξ|→+∞W⁡(ξ)=+∞;\lim_{|\xi|\to+\infty}W(\xi)=+\infty;
  2. ii)

    WW is not affine in any interval of ℝ\mathbb{R};

  3. iii)

    the global unstable set ΣG\Sigma_{G} of WW, as defined in (1.7), is a bounded open set, consisting of a finite number of open connected components, denoted by

    Σ1,…,Σℓ.\Sigma_{1},\dots,\Sigma_{\ell}.

For the standard double-well potential (1.2) one has ℓ=1\ell=1 and ΣG=Σ1=(−1,1)\Sigma_{G}=\Sigma_{1}=(-1,1).

2.2. The functionals Fε{F_{\varepsilon}}, F∗⁣∗{F^{**}}, |∇Fε||\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|, |∇F∗⁣∗||\nabla{F^{**}}|

For any ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1] we indicate by

Fε:ℋm−1​(𝕋)→[0,+∞]{F_{\varepsilon}}:{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})\to[0,+\infty]

the functional defined as

Fε(v):={∫𝕋(ε2​(vx)22+W⁡(v))​𝑑xif vx∈L2​(𝕋) and W​(v)∈L1​(𝕋), +∞elsewhere,{F_{\varepsilon}}(v):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}}\Big(\varepsilon^{2}\frac{(v_{x})^{2}}{2}+W(v)\Big)\,dx&\text{if $v_{x}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{T})$ and $W(v)\in L^{1}(\mathbb{T})$, }\\ +\infty&\text{elsewhere},\end{cases}

and by

F∗⁣∗:ℋm−1​(𝕋)→[0,+∞]{F^{**}}:{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})\to[0,+\infty]

the functional defined as

F∗⁣∗​(v):={∫𝕋W∗⁣∗​(v)​𝑑xif​W∗⁣∗​(v)∈L1​(𝕋),+∞elsewhere.{F^{**}}(v):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}}W^{**}(v)~dx&{\rm if}~W^{**}(v)\in L^{1}(\mathbb{T}),\\ +\infty&{\rm elsewhere}.\end{cases}

It is clear that F∗⁣∗{F^{**}} is a convex functional.

We denote by

|∇Fε|:ℋm−1​(𝕋)→[0,+∞]|\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|\colon{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})\to[0,+\infty]

the functional defined as

|∇Fε|​(v):={‖(W′​(v)−ε2​vx​x)x‖L2​(𝕋)if Fε​(v)<+∞ and(W′​(v)−ε2​vx​x)x∈L2​(𝕋),+∞elsewhere,|\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|(v):=\begin{cases}\|\ (W^{\prime}(v)-\varepsilon^{2}v_{xx})_{x}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T})}&\text{if ${F_{\varepsilon}}(v)<+\infty$ and}\\ {}&\text{$(W^{\prime}(v)-\varepsilon^{2}v_{xx})_{x}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{T})$},\\ \\ +\infty&\text{elsewhere},\end{cases}

and by

|∇F∗⁣∗|:ℋm−1​(𝕋)→[0,+∞]|\nabla{F^{**}}|:{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})\to[0,+\infty]

the functional defined as

|∇F∗⁣∗|(v):={∥(W∗∗′(v))x∥L2​(𝕋)if F∗⁣∗​(v)<+∞ and (W∗∗′(v))x∈L2(𝕋),+∞elsewhere.|\nabla{F^{**}}|(v):=\begin{cases}\|(W^{**~\!\prime}(v))_{x}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T})}&\text{if ${F^{**}}(v)<+\infty$ and $(W^{**~\!\prime}(v))_{x}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{T})$},\\ +\infty&\text{elsewhere}.\end{cases}

3. Statement of the main result

Given ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1] and u¯ε∈ℋm−1​(𝕋)\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}\in{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) such that

Fε​(u¯ε)<+∞,{F_{\varepsilon}}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon})<+\infty,

we let uε∈𝒞∞((0,+∞)×𝕋)∩𝒞0([0,+∞);ℋm−1(𝕋)){u_{\varepsilon}}\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}((0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{T})\cap\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,+\infty);{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})) be the solution to the Cauchy problem

{ut=(W′​(u)−ε2​ux​x)x​xin (0,+∞)×𝕋,u=u¯εon {0}×𝕋.\begin{cases}{\rm u}_{t}=\Big(W^{\prime}({\rm u})-\varepsilon^{2}{\rm u}_{xx}\Big)_{xx}&\text{in~ $(0,+\infty)\times{\mathbb{T}}$},\\ {\rm u}~=\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}&\text{on $\{0\}\times{\mathbb{T}}$}.\end{cases} (3.1)

We notice that uε{u_{\varepsilon}} is the gradient flow of Fε{F_{\varepsilon}} in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) starting at u¯ε\overline{u}_{\varepsilon} in the sense of [1], that is, it satisfies:

  • -

    uε∈AC2([0,+∞);ℋm−1(𝕋)){u_{\varepsilon}}\in AC^{2}\left([0,+\infty);{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})\right), where AC2([0,+∞);ℋm−1(𝕋))AC^{2}\left([0,+\infty);{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})\right) denotes the space of absolutely continuous curves from [0,+∞)[0,+\infty) to ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) having derivative in L2​((,,,))L^{2}((0,+\infty)),

  • -

    (0,+∞)∋t↦|∇Fε|​(uε​(t))(0,+\infty)\ni t\mapsto|\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|({u_{\varepsilon}}(t)) belongs to L2​((,,,))L^{2}((0,+\infty)),

  • -

    for all t≥0t\geq 0

    Fε​(u¯ε)=Fε​(uε​(t))+12​∫0t‖∂tuε​(s)‖−12​𝑑s+12​∫0t|∇Fε|2​(uε​(s))​𝑑s.{F_{\varepsilon}}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon})={F_{\varepsilon}}({u_{\varepsilon}}(t))+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{t}{u_{\varepsilon}}(s)\|_{-1}^{2}\,ds+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}|\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|^{2}({u_{\varepsilon}}(s))\,ds. (3.2)

A differential characterization of the gradient flow of F∗⁣∗{F^{**}} in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) is more delicate, as regularity issues appear. Indeed, the function W∗⁣∗W^{**} is just of class 𝒞1,1​(ℝ)\mathcal{C}^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}), and not of class 𝒞2​(ℝ)\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}). Yet it is possible to see that |∇F∗⁣∗||\nabla{F^{**}}| is a strong upper gradient for F∗⁣∗{F^{**}} in the sense of [1, Definition 1.2.1], so that from the general theory of maximal monotone operators (see for instance [4, Theorem 3.2]) one gets the following result.

Proposition 3.1 (Gradient flow of F∗⁣∗{F^{**}}).

Let u¯∈ℋm−1​(𝕋)\overline{u}\in{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) be such that

F∗⁣∗​(u¯)<+∞.{F^{**}}(\overline{u})<+\infty.

Then there exists a unique gradient flow solution uu of F∗⁣∗{F^{**}} starting at u¯\overline{u}, which satisfies

  • -

    u∈AC2([0,+∞);ℋm−1(𝕋))u\in AC^{2}\left([0,+\infty);{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})\right),

  • -

    (0,+∞)∋t↦|∇F∗⁣∗|(u⁡(t))(0,+\infty)\ni t\mapsto|\nabla{F^{**}}|(u(t)) belongs to L2​((,,,))L^{2}((0,+\infty)),

  • -

    for all t≥0t\geq 0

    F∗⁣∗​(u¯)=F∗⁣∗​(u⁡(t))+12​∫0t‖∂tu⁡(s)‖−12​𝑑s+12​∫0t|∇F∗⁣∗|2​(u⁡(s))​𝑑s.{F^{**}}(\overline{u})={F^{**}}(u(t))+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial_{t}u(s)\|_{-1}^{2}\,ds+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}|\nabla{F^{**}}|^{2}(u(s))\,ds. (3.3)

Note that uu solves equation (1.6) in the sense of distributions.

We are now in the position to state the main result of this paper.

Theorem 3.2 (Convergence of solutions).

Let u¯ε,u¯∈ℋm−1​(𝕋)\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\,\overline{u}\in{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) be such that

Fε​(u¯ε)<+∞,F∗⁣∗​(u¯)<+∞.{F_{\varepsilon}}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon})<+\infty,\qquad{F^{**}}(\overline{u})<+\infty.

Suppose that

limε↓0u¯ε=u¯in​ℋm−1​(𝕋)\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}=\overline{u}\qquad{\rm in}~{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) (3.4)

and

limε↓0Fε​(u¯ε)=F∗⁣∗​(u¯).\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}~{F_{\varepsilon}}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon})={F^{**}}(\overline{u}). (3.5)

Then for any T>0T>0,

limε↓0uε=uin​𝒞0​([0,T],ℋm−1​(𝕋))\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}{u_{\varepsilon}}=u\quad{\rm in}~\mathcal{C}^{0}([0,T];{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T})) (3.6)

and

limε↓0∫0T(|∇Fε|​(uε​(t))−|∇F∗⁣∗|​(u⁡(t)))2​𝑑t=0.\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\int_{0}^{T}\Big(|\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|({u_{\varepsilon}}(t))-|\nabla{F^{**}}|(u(t))\Big)^{2}~dt=0.

In particular

limε↓0Fε​(uε​(t))=F∗⁣∗​(u⁡(t)),t≥0.\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}{F_{\varepsilon}}({u_{\varepsilon}}(t))={F^{**}}(u(t)),\qquad t\geq 0.

As already mentioned, following [17], the main ingredient to prove Theorem 3.2 is the following (time independent) result, which concerns the Γ\Gamma-limit of the slope in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) of the functionals Fε{F_{\varepsilon}}.

Theorem 3.3 (Γ\Gamma-liminf of (|∇Fε|)(|\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|)).

Let v∈ℋm−1​(𝕋)v\in{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) and let (vε)(v_{\varepsilon}) be a sequence in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) such that

limε↓0vε=vin​ℋm−1​(𝕋)\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}v_{\varepsilon}=v\qquad{\rm in}~{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) (3.7)

and

We expect a full Γ\Gamma-convergence result to hold for (|∇Fε|)(|\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|), however such result is not needed in order to prove Theorem 3.2.

(4.1)

In the next lemma we introduce a parametrized family μ\mu of probability measures, associated with suitable sequences (vε)(v_{\varepsilon}), the so-called Young measures. If λ:𝕋∋x↦λx∈𝒫⁡(ℝ)\lambda:\mathbb{T}\ni x\mapsto\lambda_{x}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}) is a parametrized family of probability measures, by λ⁡(f)\lambda(f) we mean the function 𝕋∋x↦λx​(f)∈ℝ\mathbb{T}\ni x\mapsto\lambda_{x}(f)\in\mathbb{R}.

As a consequence of Proposition 4.6 we have the following result which, roughly speaking, says that the oscillations of a sequence (vε)(v_{\varepsilon}) satisfying (4.3), if contained in a connected component of ℝ∖ΣL,\mathbb{R}\setminus\Sigma_{L}, namely in an interval where W′W^{\prime} is monotone, are damped down. This result should be considered together with Lemma 5.3 of Section 5, which gives further informations on μx​(W∗⁣∗′)\mu_{x}({W^{**}}^{\prime}).

Corollary 4.7 (Support of μx\mu_{x}, I).

Let μ\mu be as in Lemma 4.5. For almost every x∈𝕋x\in\mathbb{T} for which spt⁡(μx){\rm spt}(\mu_{x}) is contained in a connected component of ℝ∖ΣL\mathbb{R}\setminus\Sigma_{L}, we have that μx\mu_{x} is a Dirac delta.

Proof.

Since the intervals where W′W^{\prime} is strictly monotone are at most countable, we can fix an interval II where W′W^{\prime} is strictly increasing, and suppose that there exists a set A⊆𝕋A\subseteq\mathbb{T} of positive measure so that for almost every x∈Ax\in A the support of μx\mu_{x} is contained in II. Choose now a nondecreasing continuous function ll so that l=W′l=W^{\prime} in II. Then from (4.12) it follows

μx​(W′2)≤(μx​(W′))2a.e.x∈A,\mu_{x}(W^{\prime 2})\leq(\mu_{x}(W^{\prime}))^{2}\qquad{\rm a.e.}~x\in A,

which is a reverse Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. It follows that W′W^{\prime} is constant μx\mu_{x}-almost everywhere in AA, and the thesis follows recalling that, by assumption, WW is not affine in any interval. ∎

5. Localization of oscillations

The information gained from the results of the previous section, and in particular from Corollary 4.7, are not enough to conclude the proof of Theorem 3.3. Our aim now (see Lemma 5.3) is to prove that for almost every x∈𝕋x\in\mathbb{T}, either μx\mu_{x} is a Dirac delta or its support is contained in the closure of a connected component of ΣG\Sigma_{G}. The following result, heavily relying on the one-dimensional setting, is the crucial step toward the proof of this assertion.

For any ρ>0\rho>0 define

ΣGρ:={ξ∈ℝ:dist⁡(ξ,ΣG)<ρ}.\Sigma_{G}^{\rho}:=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}:{\rm dist}(\xi,\Sigma_{G})<\rho\}.
Lemma 5.1 (Localization of oscillations, I).

Let vε∈ℋm−1​(𝕋)v_{\varepsilon}\in{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) and c∈(0,+∞)c\in(0,+\infty) be such that

Fε​(vε)+|∇Fε|​(vε)≤c,ε∈(0,1].{F_{\varepsilon}}(v_{\varepsilon})+|\nabla{F_{\varepsilon}}|(v_{\varepsilon})\leq c,\qquad\varepsilon\in(0,1]. (5.1)

For any η>0\eta>0 there exists δ=δ⁡(η,c)>0\delta=\delta(\eta,c)>0, depending on η\eta and cc, but independent of ε\varepsilon, such that for any pair xε∈𝕋x_{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{T}, yε∈𝕋y_{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{T} of points satisfying the properties

  • (i)

    0<yε−xε≤δ0<y_{\varepsilon}-x_{\varepsilon}\leq\delta,

  • (ii)

    vεx​(xε)=vεx​(yε)=0{v_{\varepsilon}}_{x}(x_{\varepsilon})={v_{\varepsilon}}_{x}(y_{\varepsilon})=0,

we have either

vε​(z)∈ΣGη,z∈[xε,yε]v_{\varepsilon}(z)\in\Sigma_{G}^{\eta},\qquad z\in[x_{\varepsilon},y_{\varepsilon}] (5.2)

or

|vε​(yε)−vε​(xε)|<η.|v_{\varepsilon}(y_{\varepsilon})-v_{\varepsilon}(x_{\varepsilon})|<\eta. (5.3)
Remark 5.2.

Before proving Lemma 5.1, some comments are in order. First of all remember that (5.1) implies (Remark 4.3) that vε∈H3​(𝕋)v_{\varepsilon}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{T}), and therefore vεv_{\varepsilon} are Hölder continuous (in particular uniformly continuous). This fact, provided we assume 0<yε−xε≤δ0<y_{\varepsilon}-x_{\varepsilon}\leq\delta, does not imply inequality (5.3), since η\eta is required not to depend on ε\varepsilon. The second observation concerns the meaning of Lemma 5.1: this lemma states, roughly speaking, that between two stationary points the functions vεv_{\varepsilon} either have a small oscillation, or they must be close to the set ΣG\Sigma_{G} of the ε\varepsilon-independent quantity η\eta. In some sense, if vεv_{\varepsilon} have a sufficiently large excursion between two critical points, their values cannot lie inside the region where WW is convex. Finally, the qualitative behavior of δ\delta in dependence of η\eta is explicit to a certain extent, see (5.18) below.

Appendix A

For completeness, in this appendix we quickly prove here a Γ\Gamma-convergence result concerning the functionals Fε{F_{\varepsilon}}. This result is unnecessary for the proof of Theorem 3.2.

Proposition A.1 (Γ\Gamma-limit of Fε{F_{\varepsilon}}).

The sequence (Fε)({F_{\varepsilon}}) Γ\Gamma-converges to F∗⁣∗{F^{**}} in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0.

Proof.

The functional F∗⁣∗{F^{**}} is lower semicontinuous in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}). We now prove the Γ\Gamma-limsup inequality: given v∈ℋm−1​(𝕋)v\in{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) we have to find a sequence (vε)⊂ℋm−1​(𝕋)(v_{\varepsilon})\subset{\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) with

such that

limε↓0Fε​(vε)→F⁡(v)as​ε↓0.\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}{F_{\varepsilon}}(v_{\varepsilon})\to F(v)\quad{\rm as}~\varepsilon\downarrow 0. (A.2)

Assume first that vv is piecewise constant and takes values in ℝ∖ΣG\mathbb{R}\setminus\Sigma_{G}. It is now enough to show that the class of functions vv considered above is dense in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) and with respect to F∗⁣∗{F^{**}}, so that the thesis will follow by a standard density argument. Since piecewise constant functions are dense in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}), it is sufficient to show that a piecewise constant function vv can be approximated in ℋm−1​(𝕋){\mathcal{H}^{-1}_{m}}(\mathbb{T}) by piecewise constant functions vnv_{n} taking values in ℝ∖ΣG\mathbb{R}\setminus\Sigma_{G} and such that

Let vv be piecewise constant. Let A⊆𝕋A\subseteq\mathbb{T} be an interval where vv takes value in (a,b)(a,b), with (a,b)(a,b) a connected component of ΣG\Sigma_{G}. since W∗⁣∗W^{**} is linear on [a,b][a,b]. We can apply the same argument in the intervals where vv takes values in ΣG\Sigma_{G}, while we keep vn=vv_{n}=v in the rest of the domain. This concludes the proof. ∎
